case_study_insert.main_stem: Swiftclean Laundry Services (SLS) is a private limited company in the commercial laundry and dry-cleaning sector, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2008 by Grace Mensah, the business cleans hotel uniform bundles and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. SLS plans to invest $720,000 in a new automated washing line with a water-recycling system, financed by a $450,000 eight-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $12 a unit and a selling price of $27, and currently produces 30,000 units a year. SLS faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 7% and a growing number of hotels report stained uniforms needing rewash.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: SLS processed 7,500 uniform bundles last quarter with a rewash rate of 2.8%, down from 4.1% a year ago. Complaints about stained uniforms fell from 31 to 12 per month. Average turnaround is 3.4 days. A survey of 350 hotel managers found that 66% would pay up to $0.90 more per bundle for water-recycled cleaning, and 58% check environmental practices when choosing a laundry supplier.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Swiftclean Laundry Services for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.4% to 5.3%. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $12.60 to $13.41 per hour from April 2027. (3) Energy and detergent input costs have risen 10.4% year-on-year, laundry services inflation is 5.9%, and hotel outsourcing spending grew 2.6% in the same period.

questions.question_text: SLS is funding part of its $720,000 washing line with a $450,000 eight-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for SLS of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit has no interest or repayment burden, so the $270,000 provided internally is cheaper than the $450,000 eight-year bank loan. The money saved can be spent on tackling the 2.8% rewash rate and on covering the $300,000 a year fixed costs, protecting the $27 selling price and the cash needed to pay 55 staff while 7% absenteeism reduces capacity.

Point 2: Using internal funds keeps ownership and control with Grace Mensah rather than a lender, so no bank can impose conditions on how the water-recycling line is operated or on which hotels are served. With a hierarchical structure, this avoids another external approval layer and there is no asset at risk if hotel contracts slip; SLS can use the full benefit of the $720,000 investment to answer the 31-to-12 fall in stained-uniform complaints.

This is valuable while stained bundles require rewash and use extra capacity, and it avoids regular repayments that would compete with the cost of detergents and machine maintenance.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to SLS and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: SLS is promoting its new water-recycled cleaning service to hotels. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should SLS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television campaign: A national TV advert could build awareness of water-recycled cleaning among hotel chains and support the $720,000 washing line. However, production and airtime are very expensive for a 55-employee laundry already servicing a $450,000 loan, and most viewers are not hotel procurement managers, so a large part of the spend would not reach buyers.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is far cheaper and can target the region where SLS's 3.4-day turnaround is strongest, making it suitable for a short launch message. Its weakness is geographic reach: hotel customers are spread beyond the local area, so radio alone is unlikely to generate the 30,000-unit volume required to cover $300,000 fixed costs.

Social media influencer marketing: Hospitality and sustainability influencers can demonstrate the water-recycling process to the exact hotel managers who buy laundry services, with measurable engagement and low cost per contact. It lets SLS use the survey result that 66% of 350 hotel managers would pay $0.90 more for water-recycled cleaning and 58% check environmental practices, converting Appendix 1 into a precise selling message.

Recommendation: SLS should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches hotel buyers directly, costs much less than television and travels further than local radio, and reinforces the $0.90 premium needed after the 10.4% input-cost rise. Television is rejected as unaffordable for a $450,000-loan-funded launch, and radio is rejected as too narrow for a business aiming at 30,000 units a year.

Influencer content can also be changed quickly if hotel feedback on the 3.4-day turnaround changes, which a fixed television booking cannot accommodate.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to SLS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SLS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed analysis of all three options in the context of SLS with a justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: SLS has 7% absenteeism and hotels report stained uniforms. Explain two benefits for SLS of using autocratic leadership to improve standards and motivation in its packing team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership sets clear, uniform quality rules for sorting and packing hotel bundles, so every worker follows the same staining check. In a hierarchical structure with 55 staff and a 2.8% rewash rate, unambiguous instructions reduce variation and errors, protecting the service that has already cut complaints from 31 to 12 per month.

Point 2: Decisions can be made quickly when a hotel reports a stained uniform or when 7% absenteeism leaves a shift short, because Grace Mensah can reallocate tasks without delay. Meeting hotel delivery targets protects the contracts that support 30,000 units a year and the $300,000 fixed costs; job security from keeping those accounts, plus clear expectations, gives staff a practical reason to stay motivated.

Clear promotion criteria also make the 55 staff aware of what good work looks like, supporting motivation through fair recognition, while the faster response protects the 3.4-day turnaround that hotels value.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to SLS's absenteeism, rewash rate and hotel contracts.

questions.question_text: SLS wants to reduce its 7% absenteeism and 2.8% rewash rate. Consider introducing quality circles or paying a performance-related bonus for stain-free bundles. Which should SLS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Quality circles: Regular meetings where sorters and machine operators discuss staining problems would use front-line knowledge to find causes and reduce the 2.8% rewash rate. Workers feel consulted, which can lift motivation and reduce 7% absenteeism. The approach is cheap and fits a 55-employee team, but it works slowly and clashes with the autocratic, hierarchical style in the stem unless managers genuinely delegate.

Performance-related bonus: Paying a bonus for bundles that pass the stain check gives an immediate incentive and could build on the fall in complaints from 31 to 12 per month. It is simple to attach to existing inspection records, but it costs cash each period, may encourage staff to hide errors to qualify, and does not by itself solve the absenteeism that leaves shifts short.

Decision: SLS should choose the performance-related bonus. It gives a direct, measurable reward for the specific stain-free outcome hotels care about, fits the existing top-down inspection system, and can be funded from the margins shown in Appendix 2. Quality circles are rejected because they are slow, require a participative culture SLS does not currently have, and would not quickly address the 7% absenteeism; staff consultation can be added once the bonus has stabilised quality.

There is also a cash question: SLS is committing $270,000 of retained profit to the new line, so a bonus paid each month competes with that investment and with the need to replace worn machines. A bonus can still be introduced later if stain-free results fail to improve, but at present the measurement burden and recurring cost make it the weaker choice for a 55-employee laundry with hierarchical control.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two approaches with limited application to SLS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both approaches in the context of SLS.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluation of both approaches with a justified decision covering cost, culture and measurability, explaining why the alternative is rejected.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SLS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $300,000 ÷ ($27 − $12) = $300,000 ÷ $15 = 20,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 20,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $27 − $12 = $15. Answer: contribution per unit is $15.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SLS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 20,000-unit break-even output with 30,000 units produced: the margin of safety is 10,000 bundles, showing how far hotel orders could fall before a loss while 7% absenteeism and rewash affect capacity.
2. Use the $15 contribution per unit to test the $0.90 premium from the survey: raising the $27 price to $27.90 would lift contribution to $15.90, so about 18,868 bundles would cover $300,000 fixed costs, helping set the hotel price.
3. Average total cost is $22 a unit ($300,000 ÷ 30,000 = $10 plus $12) against the $27 price, a benchmark for the new automated line and a floor in hotel contract negotiations.
4. Labour productivity is about 545 units per worker (30,000 ÷ 55); tracking it shows whether absenteeism and the 2.8% rewash rate are eroding efficiency and whether the $720,000 investment is paying off.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 20,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $15 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 10,000 units against 30,000 units output; pricing test of the $0.90 premium against $300,000 fixed costs; average total cost of $22 against the $27 price; and labour productivity of about 545 units per worker to monitor absenteeism and rewash.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SLS's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has SLS's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 42.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 16.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 18.0%

Detailed workings:
2024: revenue 800, cost of sales 520, gross profit 280; 2025: revenue 900, cost of sales 522, gross profit 378. Operating profit rose from 96 to 144 and capital employed from 640 to 800. Interest payable moved from 18 to 22.

Evaluation: The figures show a strong improvement. The trading margin rose from 35.0% to 42.0% because cost of sales was almost flat at 522 while revenue reached 900, so the rewash and staining problems were controlled. The operating margin improved from 12.0% to 16.0%, meaning the $300,000 fixed costs and 7% absenteeism were better absorbed as volume grew. Return on capital rose from 15.0% to 18.0% even though capital employed increased to 800, so the existing assets are generating more profit before the $720,000 line is added.

Conclusion: SLS's financial position has improved. All three measures are higher in 2025, so profitability and the efficiency of capital use have strengthened together, which supports servicing the $450,000 bank loan. The caution is that interest payable has risen from 18 to 22 and energy and detergent costs by 10.4%, so the improved margins must be defended through the $0.90 water-recycling premium.

The jump in gross profit from 280 to 378 is especially significant because cost of sales barely changed, implying the rewash problem was contained rather than hidden by higher prices.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of margin and capital trends and a justified conclusion on whether SLS's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SLS of introducing water-recycled cleaning for its hotel uniform bundles.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 350 hotel managers shows 66% would pay up to $0.90 more per bundle for water-recycled cleaning and 58% check environmental practices, so SLS can add a premium that raises the $15 contribution per unit and protects the improved trading margin shown in Appendix 2 against the 10.4% energy and detergent rise. It also strengthens the case for the $720,000 washing line when tendering for hotel contracts.

Disadvantage: Installing and running the water-recycling system may raise the $300,000 a year fixed costs or the $12 variable cost per unit, so the $0.90 premium must cover the extra cost or margins fall. If the system causes any delay, the 3.4-day turnaround could slip and the complaints that fell from 31 to 12 per month might rise again, especially while 7% absenteeism persists.

SLS would also need to check that the water-recycling system can handle the 7,500 bundles processed each quarter without delaying hotel deliveries.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to SLS's research, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.3%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase to $13.41 and the 10.4% rise in energy and detergent input costs will affect SLS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.4% to 5.3%): The increase is 0.9 percentage points, so if the $450,000 eight-year bank loan is variable-rate the extra cost is 0.009 × $450,000 = $4,050 a year. This is small next to $300,000 fixed costs and would be zero if the loan is fixed-rate, so SLS can reduce this risk by fixing the rate. It is the least urgent of the three changes.

Minimum wage rise (6.4% to $13.41): The insert gives no hours worked or existing pay for the 55 staff, so a defensible annual wage bill cannot be invented. The correct judgement is that the entire payroll becomes more expensive while output must stay near 30,000 bundles to cover $300,000 fixed costs; with 7% absenteeism already reducing capacity, higher labour cost per bundle can only be absorbed through higher hotel prices or the productivity of the new line.

Energy and detergent rise (10.4%): As an explicitly labelled upper bound, if the whole $12 variable cost were exposed, 0.104 × $12 = about $1.25 per bundle, or roughly $37,440 a year at 30,000 units, cutting contribution from $15 to about $13.75. Even a partial pass-through would reduce the margin available to service the $450,000 loan, though the 66% of hotel managers accepting a $0.90 premium offers some protection.

Conclusion: The 10.4% rise in energy and detergent costs has the greatest impact because it recurs on every one of the 30,000 bundles and directly erodes the $15 contribution that underpins the $720,000 investment. The interest rise is only $4,050 a year and can be fixed, while the wage effect is spread across payroll and cannot be quantified from the insert, so neither is as immediate a threat.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to SLS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on SLS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with shown derivations from insert figures and a justified greatest-impact judgment with reasons for rejecting the other two.
